Prompt:
Write an essay arguing in favor of not hunting down and executing officials who enforced a brutal regime after its fall, emphasizing that this reason alone does not sufficiently justify violence.
Model Response:

When a brutal regime collapses, the impulse to hunt down and execute the officials who enforced it can feel like moral clarity at last: the oppressors are vulnerable, the victims finally have power, and “justice” seems as simple as ending the lives of those who helped inflict suffering. But that impulse—however understandable—does not, by itself, justify violence. A society emerging from tyranny needs accountability, truth, and repair. It does not need revenge killings. Executing former officials for the mere fact that they served the regime replaces one form of political violence with another and undermines the very moral and civic foundations a post‑regime order must build.

1) “They enforced the regime” is not a sufficient moral basis for killing

The fact that someone enforced a brutal regime is a reason to investigate them, restrict their power, and assess responsibility. It is not automatically a reason to execute them. Moral responsibility comes in degrees: some designed policies of terror; some enthusiastically carried them out; some complied under coercion; some performed administrative roles with little connection to atrocities; some tried to mitigate harm from within. Collapsing all of these distinctions into a single category—“official”—treats people as interchangeable symbols of evil rather than moral agents with particular choices and acts.

Even if a society believes that certain crimes merit the harshest punishment, morally defensible punishment depends on more than affiliation. It depends on what a person did, intended, enabled, and could reasonably have refused. Killing people merely because they belonged to the machinery of rule turns accountability into collective retribution. And collective retribution is one of the hallmarks of the very brutality the new society is trying to leave behind.

2) Extrajudicial execution imitates tyranny and erodes the rule of law

A brutal regime’s defining feature is often that it treats law as a weapon and violence as a tool of governance. If the new order responds by hunting down and executing former officials outside due process, it sends a fatal message: power, not principle, determines who lives and dies. That is not justice; it is a change in who wields the gun.

The rule of law is not a luxury reserved for calm times. It is precisely what distinguishes legitimate authority from domination. Trials, evidence, defense, and judgment by an accountable court are not sentimental niceties; they are the mechanisms by which a society proves—publicly and verifiably—that it has broken with arbitrary violence. Without due process, even correct conclusions (“this person committed atrocities”) are reached by illegitimate means. And illegitimate means tend to outlive their original targets, eventually becoming the new state’s normal method of dealing with dissent.

3) Revenge violence risks a spiral that endangers victims and the future

Hunting and executing former officials rarely stays limited to the truly guilty. In practice, it invites false accusations, personal vendettas, factional score‑settling, and the targeting of family members or associates. Once killing becomes an accepted instrument of “justice,” the boundary of who deserves it expands—often quickly. The result is not closure but a spiral: yesterday’s victims become tomorrow’s perpetrators, and the new regime inherits a culture of fear and blood debt.

This spiral is not only morally corrosive; it is strategically self‑defeating. Societies recovering from authoritarianism face fragile institutions, armed groups, economic instability, and deep distrust. Extrajudicial violence adds fuel to each of these problems. It encourages underground resistance, makes reconciliation harder, and teaches everyone—including future officials—that losing power may mean death, which incentivizes them to cling to power by any means.

4) Accountability is stronger, not weaker, when it is legal and public

Rejecting execution squads does not mean excusing crimes. It means insisting that accountability be real rather than theatrical. Public trials, lustration policies, truth commissions, reparations, and institutional reforms can impose consequences while also building a factual record. A legal process can identify who ordered crimes, who profited, who had meaningful agency, and who can provide information about mass graves, torture sites, and missing persons.

This matters for victims. Many victims want more than retaliation; they want truth, acknowledgment, and guarantees of non‑repetition. A dead official may satisfy a moment of rage, but a documented verdict can expose networks, recover stolen assets, clarify chains of command, and establish an authoritative history that denialists cannot easily erase. In that sense, lawful accountability can be both more humane and more effective than vigilante execution.

5) The new society must model the ethics it claims to embrace

A post‑brutal society often declares that human dignity is inviolable, that citizens are not disposable, and that violence should not substitute for argument or law. Executing former officials because they “deserve it” risks making those principles conditional—granted to some and withdrawn from others. But principles that only apply to the innocent are not principles; they are preferences.

If the new order wants citizens to believe that rights are universal, it must demonstrate that universality at the hardest moments—especially when dealing with hated figures. Showing restraint is not weakness; it is an ethical claim made concrete: that even those associated with evil will be judged by standards rather than slaughtered by anger.

6) “They enforced it” may explain wrongdoing, but explanation is not permission

It is important to acknowledge why the urge for violent retribution arises. Survivors may feel abandoned by courts, betrayed by neighbors, and desperate for recognition. In such conditions, execution can appear like the only language oppressors understand. Yet the emotional intelligibility of revenge is not a moral warrant for it. Explanation—“people are furious and traumatized”—does not become permission—“therefore killing is justified.”

Moreover, the category “enforced the regime” is broad enough to ensnare people who were themselves coerced, threatened, or trapped. Many authoritarian systems deliberately compromise ordinary workers—clerks, teachers, low‑level police, local administrators—so that guilt becomes widely distributed and society becomes easier to control. A policy of hunting down “enforcers” can end up punishing those whom the regime already victimized, while the most culpable flee, bargain, or hide behind chaos.

7) A better alternative: firm, individualized, nonviolent justice

A principled refusal to execute former officials should be paired with concrete measures that take victims seriously:

  • Secure arrests and detention under law, with oversight to prevent torture and disappearance.
  • Individualized prosecutions for those who ordered or committed grave crimes, using transparent standards of evidence.
  • Disqualification from power for key regime figures where appropriate (lustration), with clear criteria and appeal mechanisms.
  • Truth‑seeking processes to document abuses, locate victims, and counter denial.
  • Reparations and restitution, including recovery of stolen assets.
  • Institutional reform of security services and courts to prevent old practices from reemerging.

These measures treat wrongdoing as something to be proven and answered for, not something to be avenged indiscriminately. They also keep society oriented toward building institutions rather than feeding a cycle of bloodshed.

Conclusion

The fall of a brutal regime is a moment when a society chooses what it will become. Killing former officials simply because they enforced the old order may feel like justice, but it is not justified by that reason alone—and it carries moral and practical costs that can poison the future. A new society honors victims and defeats tyranny more fully by refusing to mirror the regime’s contempt for life and law. Accountability is necessary; violence is not. The strongest break from brutality is to insist that even those who served it are confronted with truth and judged by fair procedures, not hunted down and executed by rage.
